title: The Pirates' Articles
text:
Bartholomew Roberts, a Welsh sailor forced into piracy when his ship was captured in 1719, became one of the most successful pirates of his age, taking hundreds of ships off Africa, Brazil and the Caribbean. His crew was large and drawn from many places. To keep it working together, they lived under a written set of articles that each man signed or swore to.

The book A General History of the Pyrates, published in 1724 under the name Captain Charles Johnson, reproduces Roberts's articles. Every man had a vote in affairs of importance and an equal right to fresh food and drink when captured. Gambling for money was forbidden. Lights and candles had to be out at eight at night. Each man had to keep his weapons clean and ready. Fighting among the crew on board was banned; quarrels had to be settled ashore, by duel. A man who deserted his post in battle could be killed or marooned.

Shares of plunder were set in advance: the captain and quartermaster received two shares, a few officers one and a half or one and a quarter, and everyone else one. A man who lost a limb in service received a fixed compensation from the common fund. The musicians had the Sabbath off.

Roberts was killed in battle with a British warship off the coast of Africa in February 1722. Many of his crew were tried and hanged.
lesson: Even outlaws need fair shares, clear rules and a voice for every member to work together. Agreements made in the open are what hold a team together.
location: Atlantic Ocean, West Africa and the Caribbean
source: Captain Charles Johnson, A General History of the Robberies and Murders of the Most Notorious Pyrates (1724), chapter on Bartholomew Roberts
caveat: The author 'Charles Johnson' is unidentified, and some details of his book may be embellished.
